title: try_read_command_ascii's leading-space skip has no end, so a read buffer of nothing but spaces walks the cursor off the cache object
object: c->rbuf, a cache.c object of READ_BUFFER_SIZE taken by do_cache_alloc(c->thread->rbuf_cache) at memcached.c:408
lifetime_ender: NONE -- the buffer is alive throughout. SPATIAL.
shape: `while (*ptr == ' ') { ++ptr; }` with no end condition, over a buffer whose branch premise is that it contains no '\n'; a buffer of nothing but spaces therefore walks the cursor past the object and on into the next object of the same cache
allocator_layer: cache.c, the object cache, over pages the slab allocator owns. An inner allocator carved the crossed region, so under this inventory's axis -- WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT -- this row IS NESTED.
nested_why: an inner allocator (cache.c) carved the crossed region out of a larger page it had itself obtained, so under this inventory's axis -- WHO ALLOCATED THE OBJECT -- this row IS NESTED.
fidelity: real allocator, model consumer. cache_create/cache_alloc/cache_free are upstream's own cache.c through this corpus's seam, and the two objects' ORDER is checked rather than assumed -- the free list promises no ascending addresses, and case 5 records the same trap costing it a refused control run. READ_BUFFER_SIZE is 16384, unreduced. The scan is upstream's own loop; only a reduction-side step cap is added so a runaway cannot hang the harness, and it is set well past the crossing so it cannot mask it. The successor object is filled with spaces too, deliberately: that is what makes the scan CONTINUE past the end rather than stop at the first byte, which is the difference between an overrun and a single stray read.
live_proof: read from the PINNED source, not from ancestry: 1.6.45:proto_text.c contains the fixed `ptr != end` 1 time and the pre-fix unbounded `while (*ptr == ' ') {` 0 times. Two-sided, so the probe is known to fire. A fix-reversal; the convention is at README.md:132-135.
distinguishing: the corpus's FOURTH spatial row and the FIRST whose object comes from cache.c rather than slabs.c -- cases 5, 6 and 7 all cross a slab chunk. That matters because the two allocators are different inner layers over the same pages, and a port that narrows one does not thereby narrow the other. It is also the only row here whose crossing distance is unbounded by construction: the scan runs for as long as the bytes beyond the object happen to be spaces, rather than by a fixed one or three bytes.

cheribsd-revocation.target: stock CheriBSD purecap with libc revocation on
cheribsd-revocation.oracle: MEASURED 2026-10-07: **CAUGHT -- which REFUTES this arm's prediction.** exit=162, FAULT signal=34, si_code=1 (BOUNDS), pc=0x105530. The arm predicted a COMPLETION on the reasoning that the crossing leaves the cache OBJECT but stays inside the page cache.c carved it from. That reasoning assumed cache.c sub-allocates objects out of pages the way slabs.c carves chunks. **It does not on this port**, and the port's own source says so: ports/memcached/allocators/src/cheribsd/malloc-leases.c:79 takes a slab PAGE with `void *page = malloc(size)`, while :161 takes each cache OBJECT with its own `void *object = malloc(size)`. So an object crossing leaves a real malloc bound, and CHERI sees it. THE REFUTATION IS WORTH MORE THAN THE PREDICTION WOULD HAVE BEEN, because it separates the corpus's two inner layers under CHERI rather than lumping them: cases 5, 6 and 7 cross a SLAB CHUNK and complete, because the chunk's crossing stays inside the one malloc the page came from; case 8 crosses a CACHE OBJECT and faults, because each object is its own malloc. 'memcached is 0 of 9 on CheriBSD' would have been the wrong summary -- it is 0 of 8 and 1 of 1, split by which inner allocator carved the storage. The platform controls and the revocation control all PASSED in the same boot, so this is a reading: cheribsd-abi, cheribsd-bounds, and revocation-control faulting as it must. RE-MEASURED 2026-10-10, results/2026-10-10-cheribsd-fixed-buggy/ (R1, pre-registered at dba29812b295): buggy SIGPROT si_code 1 at mc_case_body+0x1e8 -- inside the fault site declared before the run (case.json fault_sites) -- and the FIXED arm, the same program in the same boot, completes. The catch was a bare pc until then.
